title: 2013 Dispatched Study Abroad Report: University of Pennsylvania, USA
paragraphs: What I gained from this study abroad is a goal for learning English as a physician, an awareness of social values, and friends. After entering university, I learned the joy of research under Dr. 武川睦寛 (now a professor at the University of Tokyo), and thanks to the support of the excellent system of the Nagoya University School of Medicine, I was able to do two internships in American laboratories during long vacations. Seeing that the bridge from basic research to clinical application is strengthened even more than in Japan, I vaguely thought that next I would like to see clinical practice. Then an experience in the polyclinic became the trigger for my interest in differences in healthcare systems, starting from the question of "why are the drugs available for treatment different from country to country?", and this time I was allowed to study abroad for two months at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, a city in the eastern United States.

For the first week after the clerkship began, I felt as if I were in a storm of medicine and English. But after I remembered that I had wanted to study abroad precisely because there were things I did not know and could not do, learning became enjoyable and I was able to spend fulfilling days. At first I desperately read the guidelines and papers handed to me almost every day, but with this change of mind I began to look into things that caught my interest myself, and to search the literature as if hunting for treasure. Then I began to receive much advice and feedback from those around me, and although it was still hard, I no longer felt language and cultural differences to be a negative in terms of communication. It was at that time that I got a clue about how to study English from now on as a physician. Our team encountered an extremely rare case, and a report from Japan was adopted as the treatment policy. It is often said that English has become the common language of the world in the field of science. This time, by presenting my own experiences and thoughts in English, I began to take logical writing in English as my own problem and goal, thinking that it might help someone somewhere far away.

Being able to experience foreign medicine itself was also very meaningful in clarifying my own values. Learning cutting-edge medicine and research is of course important. However, in present-day Japan, taking in the excellent medical and educational systems of foreign countries is also considered more and more necessary in order to contribute to patients and, by extension, to society as a whole. On the other hand, during my stay I realized how much such social systems are two sides of the same coin with culture and social values. Looking back, the moment when we come into contact with something different is the chance to think about our own identity and change ourselves, and I feel that such an experience was valuable both as an individual and as a future healthcare professional facing healthcare reform that cannot wait.

I was also able to enjoy my time outside the clerkship thanks to the friends I made there. Enjoying cherry blossom viewing in Fairmount Park, where a thousand cherry trees bloom, snacks on the way back from the clerkship, and outings to the cinema, we talked not only about trivial things but also about the culture and systems of our respective countries, which are very good memories, and even after returning to Japan we keep in touch and encourage one another. I went to the United States knowing almost nothing about the city of Philadelphia, but it is a charming city whose center is surrounded by rivers flowing to the west and east, and the attractions are endless: the historic district with beautiful cobblestones, the vast campus of the university with its lovely greenery, and important cultural institutions such as the Barnes Collection and the Philadelphia Museum of Art, famous from the Rocky movies. The photograph was taken when I went to hear the Philadelphia Orchestra perform. After the clerkship ended, I toured eastern cities, Boston, New York and Washington, visiting doctors and friends who had looked after me during my earlier stay. Among them, the visit to the National Institutes of Health to which Dr. 佐藤和秀, who is studying abroad from respiratory medicine, invited me left a strong impression. Numerous buildings were scattered in a forest where wild animals live, and I was simply overwhelmed by a scale greater than I had imagined.

The six years that I thought were long are finally coming to an end. From now on too, with the positivity I cultivated by jumping into a foreign country, I will do my best while enjoying myself! With my gratitude to everyone.
